title: What no-take marine reserves do: bigger and more numerous fish, spillover, time to recover, enforcement and tourism

sources.title: When Is Spillover from Marine Reserves Likely to Benefit Fisheries?
Large Recovery of Fish Biomass in a No-Take Marine Reserve
Network of small no-take marine reserves reveals greater abundance and body size of fisheries target species
sources.license: Open access article; only facts are used

facts.text: In no-take marine reserves, where all fishing is banned, fish usually become more numerous and reach a larger average size than in fished areas.
Spillover is the movement of fish from a reserve into nearby fished waters, where they can be caught.
Recovery inside a reserve takes time; at Cabo Pulmo in Mexico, fish biomass rose more than fourfold over about a decade.
Cabo Pulmo's recovery was credited to strong local leadership and effective enforcement by residents, and it brought income from small tourism businesses such as diving.
A net benefit to fisheries from spillover is not guaranteed; it is most likely where fish stocks were heavily overfished.
